claim: Frequencies of topo I-reactive B cells (topo I-PE+ topo I-APC+ cells) in CD27+ CD19+ cells were significantly higher in anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients (n = 111) than in healthy individuals (n = 50) and anti-CENP antibody-positive SSc patients (n = 50; p<0.001).
source: Frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD27+ CD19+ cells in the peripheral blood were examined with flow cytometric analysis. Their frequencies were significantly higher in anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients (n = 111) than in healthy individuals (n = 50) and anti-CENP antibody-positive SSc patients (n = 50; p<0.001; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric data presented in Figure 1A showing statistical comparison (p<0.001) between patient groups.

claim: The mean number of topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells in the peripheral blood was 22 ± 21 cells/ml.
source: Moreover, the mean number of topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells in the peripheral blood was 22 ± 21 cells/ml.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported from the study's data.

claim: In the conventional method, 104 B cells are required to determine the concentration of cytokines produced by B cells.
source: In the conventional method, 104 B cells are required to determine the concentration of cytokines produced by B cells, which means that 500–50,000 ml of blood is needed to obtain the sufficient number of topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells for the analysis.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about conventional cytokine detection methods.

claim: Only topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD27+ CD19+ cells from anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients produced IgG anti-topo I antibodies with an average titer of +6 SD or higher.
source: We found that only topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD27+ CD19+ cells from anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients produced IgG anti-topo I antibodies with an average titer of +6 SD or higher, but these B cells from healthy individuals or anti-CENP antibody-positive SSc patients did not produce IgG anti-topo I antibodies (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by μELISA measurements shown in Figure 1B comparing antibody production across patient groups.

claim: Expression of IL2, IL6, IL10, IL14, IL16, IL23, IL35, and TGFB1 was detected in topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells from anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients.
source: Expression of IL2, IL6, IL10, IL14, IL16, IL23, IL35, and TGFB1 was detected in topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells from anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell PCR data presented in Figure 1C showing cytokine mRNA expression.

claim: Most B cells produced mainly one type of cytokines, and only a few B cells produced multiple types of cytokines.
source: Interestingly, most B cells produced mainly one type of cytokines, and only a few B cells produced multiple types of cytokines.
evidence: This observation is inferred from the single-cell PCR data patterns shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Topo I-non-reactive CD27+ B cells showed almost no expression of cytokines under unstimulated conditions.
source: In contrast, topo I-non-reactive CD27+ B cells used as a control showed almost no expression of these cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap data in Figure 1C comparing topo I-reactive and non-reactive B cells.

claim: Both topo I-reactive and topo I-non-reactive B cells stimulated ex vivo produced multiple cytokines, and the difference between them found under unstimulated conditions was lost.
source: Moreover, both topo I-reactive and topo I-non-reactive B cells stimulated ex vivo produced multiple cytokines, and the difference between them found under unstimulated conditions was lost (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing cytokine profiles before and after PMA/ionomycin stimulation in Figure 1D.

claim: Topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells are already stimulated by self-antigens in vivo.
source: These results suggest that topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells are already stimulated by self-antigens in vivo, and that this affects the difference in cytokine profiles between topo I-reactive B cells and non-reactive B cells under unstimulated conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential cytokine expression patterns observed between reactive and non-reactive B cells.

claim: B cells exposed to an antigen in vivo will increase their affinity for the antigen by somatic hypermutation until the antigen is eliminated.
source: Typically, B cells exposed to an antigen in vivo will increase their affinity for the antigen by somatic hypermutation until the antigen is eliminated (Meffre et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Meffre et al., 2001.

claim: Ongoing somatic hypermutation is observed for autoantibodies in human autoimmune diseases.
source: Ongoing somatic hypermutation is observed for autoantibodies in human autoimmune diseases (Elliott et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elliott et al., 2018.

claim: The high-affinity group of topo I-reactive B cells has low Kd value (high affinity) and the low-affinity group has high Kd value.
source: The high-affinity group has actually low Kd value (high affinity) and the low-affinity group has high Kd value (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Kd measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Almost all topo I-reactive CD27+ B cells were CD38-CD95+ cells.
source: Almost all of these cells were CD38-CD95+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of co-stimulatory molecules (CD80/86, ICOSL, and CD40) in topo I-reactive B cells with low or high affinity for topo I in anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients was elevated.
source: expression of co-stimulatory molecules (CD80/86, ICOSL, and CD40) in topo I-non-reactive B cells and topo I-reactive B cells (topo I-PE+Topo I-APC+CD19+CD27+) with low or high affinity for topo I in anti-topo I antibody-positive SSc patients was elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by μELISA measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The low-affinity group showed higher frequencies of B cells producing anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10 and IL-35.
source: The low-affinity group showed higher frequencies of B cells producing anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10 and IL-35, while the high-affinity group exhibited higher frequencies of B cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines, IL-6 and IL-23.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pie charts in Figure 2B showing cytokine-producing cell frequencies.

claim: The high-affinity group exhibited higher frequencies of B cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines, IL-6 and IL-23.
source: The low-affinity group showed higher frequencies of B cells producing anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10 and IL-35, while the high-affinity group exhibited higher frequencies of B cells producing pro-inflammatory cytokines, IL-6 and IL-23.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pie charts in Figure 2B showing cytokine-producing cell frequencies.

claim: The production of IL-6 and IL-23 was significantly higher in the high-affinity group than in the low-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively).
source: The production of IL-6 and IL-23 was significantly higher in the high-affinity group than in the low-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively); conversely, the low-affinity group exhibited significantly higher production of IL-10 and IL-35 relative to the high-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell protein measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The low-affinity group exhibited significantly higher production of IL-10 and IL-35 relative to the high-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively).
source: The production of IL-6 and IL-23 was significantly higher in the high-affinity group than in the low-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively); conversely, the low-affinity group exhibited significantly higher production of IL-10 and IL-35 relative to the high-affinity group (p<0.005, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell protein measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the amount of IL-2 and TGF-β1 production between the low-affinity and high-affinity groups.
source: There was no significant difference in the amount of IL-2 and TGF-β1 production between the two groups.
evidence: This is shown in the cytokine production data in Figure 2C.

claim: In IL-10-producing B cells, intracellular signaling and NF-kB signaling were reduced, and were mediated by p38 kinase, Jak1, Stat3, and ATF1 transcription factor.
source: In IL-10-producing B cells, intracellular signaling and NF-kB signaling were reduced, and were mediated by p38 kinase, Jak1, Stat3, and ATF1 transcription factor.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation heatmap analysis in Figure 2D showing relationships between IL-10 and intracellular proteins.

claim: IL-35-producing regulatory B cells were related to EOLA1 activation, which inhibits IL-6 signaling, HPK1, which terminate signaling cascade, and Fos transcription factor.
source: Similarly, IL-35-producing regulatory B cells were related to EOLA1 activation, which inhibits IL-6 signaling, HPK1, which terminate signaling cascade, and Fos transcription factor.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation heatmap analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: IL-6-producing effector B cells were associated with themis2 and HCST, which strengthen signaling pathway, BRAF, KICSTOR complex, SYK, FYN, STAT1, and NFkB2 transcription factor.
source: IL-6-producing effector B cells were associated with themis2 and HCST, which strengthen signaling pathway, BRAF, KICSTOR complex, SYK, FYN, STAT1, and NFkB2 transcription factor.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation heatmap analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: IL-23-producing B cells were associated with RAF1, JKAMP, and CRTC3 transcription factors.
source: IL-23-producing B cells were associated with RAF1, JKAMP, and CRTC3 transcription factors (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation heatmap analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: CD27+ B cells with low affinity for topo I upregulated FOXP3 expression in CD4+ T cells when co-cultured in microculture plates.
source: In co-culture with the microculture plates, CD27+ B cells with low affinity for topo I upregulated FOXP3 expression in CD4+ T cells, while CD27+ B cells with high affinity for topo I upregulated RORC expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by real-time RT-PCR data in Figure 3C from microculture plate experiments.

claim: CD27+ B cells with high affinity for topo I upregulated RORC expression in CD4+ T cells when co-cultured in microculture plates.
source: In co-culture with the microculture plates, CD27+ B cells with low affinity for topo I upregulated FOXP3 expression in CD4+ T cells, while CD27+ B cells with high affinity for topo I upregulated RORC expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by real-time RT-PCR data in Figure 3C from microculture plate experiments.

claim: None of the CD27+ B cells affected FOXP3 and RORC expression when using the 96-well plate.
source: Subsequently, FOXP3 and RORC mRNA expression in CD4+ T cells was examined by real-time RT-PCR (Figure 3A); however, none of the CD27+ B cells affected FOXP3 and RORC expression using the 96-well plate.
evidence: This is shown by the lack of effect in Figure 3A when using conventional 96-well plates.

claim: The volume of culture medium is 200 μl for the 96-well plate, whereas 1 μl is sufficient for the microculture plate.
source: The volume of culture medium is 200 μl for the 96-well plate, whereas 1 μl is sufficient for the microculture plate.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the culture systems used.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies against IL-10 or IL-35 inhibited Foxp3 expression in CD4+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, neutralizing antibodies against IL-10 or IL-35 inhibited Foxp3 expression in CD4+ T cells, while anti-IL-6 or IL-23 antibodies suppressed RORγt expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Anti-IL-6 or IL-23 antibodies suppressed RORγt expression in CD4+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, neutralizing antibodies against IL-10 or IL-35 inhibited Foxp3 expression in CD4+ T cells, while anti-IL-6 or IL-23 antibodies suppressed RORγt expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mice immunized four times with topo I induced skin and lung fibrosis.
source: Mice immunized four times with topo I induced skin and lung fibrosis, whereas those immunized only once did not show skin and lung fibrosis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis of dermal thickness and lung fibrosis scores in Figure 4B.

claim: Mice immunized only once with topo I did not show skin and lung fibrosis.
source: Mice immunized four times with topo I induced skin and lung fibrosis, whereas those immunized only once did not show skin and lung fibrosis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: The frequency of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in splenic B cells was significantly increased in mice immunized both once and four times with topo I compared to non-immunized mice (p<0.01).
source: The frequency of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in splenic B cells was significantly increased in mice immunized both once and four times with topo I compared to non-immunized mice (p<0.01; Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The increase in topo I-reactive B cells was more pronounced in mice immunized four times than in those immunized once (p<0.05).
source: and the increase was more pronounced in mice immunized four times than in those immunized once (p<0.05).
evidence: This is shown by comparing frequencies between the two immunization groups in Figure 4D.

claim: Titers of IgG anti-topo I antibodies produced by topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from mice immunized four times with topo I were significantly increased compared to those immunized once (p<0.01).
source: Further analysis at the single-cell level showed that titers of IgG anti-topo I antibodies produced by topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells (100 cells) from mice immunized four times with topo I were significantly increased compared to those immunized once (100 cells; p<0.01; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell antibody titer measurements in Figure 4E.

claim: The topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cell population from mice immunized once with topo I predominantly had cells producing inhibitory cytokines, IL-10 or IL-35 (71%).
source: The topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cell population from mice immunized once with topo I predominantly had cells producing inhibitory cytokines, IL-10 or IL-35 (71%), whereas that from mice immunized four times mainly had cells producing IL-6 or IL-23 (68%; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by the pie charts in Figure 4F displaying cytokine-producing cell frequencies.

claim: The topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cell population from mice immunized four times mainly had cells producing IL-6 or IL-23 (68%).
source: The topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cell population from mice immunized once with topo I predominantly had cells producing inhibitory cytokines, IL-10 or IL-35 (71%), whereas that from mice immunized four times mainly had cells producing IL-6 or IL-23 (68%; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by the pie charts in Figure 4F displaying cytokine-producing cell frequencies.

claim: IL-10 and IL-35 levels were significantly higher in mice immunized once with topo I (p<0.005).
source: Levels of cytokine proteins by these topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells were measured at the single-cell level, showing that IL-10 and IL-35 levels were significantly higher in mice immunized once with topo I (p<0.005), while IL-6 and IL-23 levels significantly increased in mice immunized four times (p<0.005; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell cytokine measurements in Figure 4G.

claim: IL-6 and IL-23 levels significantly increased in mice immunized four times with topo I (p<0.005).
source: Levels of cytokine proteins by these topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells were measured at the single-cell level, showing that IL-10 and IL-35 levels were significantly higher in mice immunized once with topo I (p<0.005), while IL-6 and IL-23 levels significantly increased in mice immunized four times (p<0.005; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell cytokine measurements in Figure 4G.

claim: There was no difference in frequencies of IL-2 and TGF-β1-producing B cells and the amount of IL-2 and TGF-β1 between mice immunized once and those immunized four times.
source: There was no difference in frequencies of IL-2 and TGF-β1-producing B cells and the amount of IL-2 and TGF-β1 between mice immunized once and those immunized four times (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is shown in the cytokine data in Figures 4F and G.

claim: Topo I-reactive CD19+ B cells were CD38-CD95+, which were activated B cells, or germinal center B cells.
source: The same results were obtained and topo I-reactive CD19+ B cells were CD38-CD95+, which were activated B cells, or germinal center B cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The ratio of high-affinity CD27+ B cells to low-affinity CD27+ B cells correlated positively with the modified Rodnan total skin thickness score (mRTSS) (p<0.0001).
source: The ratio of high-affinity CD27+ B cells to low-affinity CD27+ B cells correlated positively with the modified Rodnan total skin thickness score (mRTSS), a semiquantitative measure of skin sclerosis (p<0.0001)
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ratio of high-affinity CD27+ B cells to low-affinity CD27+ B cells correlated inversely with the percent predicted values of forced vital capacity (%FVC; p<0.0001).
source: and inversely with the percent predicted values of forced vital capacity (%FVC; p<0.0001) and diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (%DLco; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ratio of high-affinity CD27+ B cells to low-affinity CD27+ B cells correlated inversely with diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (%DLco; p<0.0001).
source: and inversely with the percent predicted values of forced vital capacity (%FVC; p<0.0001) and diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (%DLco; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
source: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001), higher mRTSS (p<0.001), more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01), and lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) and %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
evidence: This is shown in the clinical correlation data in Table 1.

claim: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited higher mRTSS (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
source: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001), higher mRTSS (p<0.001), more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01), and lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) and %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
evidence: This is shown in the clinical correlation data in Table 1.

claim: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
source: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001), higher mRTSS (p<0.001), more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01), and lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) and %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
evidence: This is shown in the clinical correlation data in Table 1.

claim: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
source: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001), higher mRTSS (p<0.001), more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01), and lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) and %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
evidence: This is shown in the clinical correlation data in Table 1.

claim: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited lower values of %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
source: Patients in the high-affinity-dominant group exhibited longer disease duration (p<0.001), higher mRTSS (p<0.001), more frequent digital scars or ulcers (p<0.01), and lower values of %FVC (p<0.001) and %DLco (p<0.001) compared to the low-affinity B cell-dominant group.
evidence: This is shown in the clinical correlation data in Table 1.

claim: Adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from mice immunized once significantly inhibited skin and lung fibrosis compared to non-adoptively transferred mice (p<0.05).
source: Adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from mice immunized once significantly inhibited skin and lung fibrosis compared to non-adoptively transferred mice (Figure 6B; p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained after four immunizations significantly enhanced skin and lung fibrosis (p<0.05).
source: By contrast, topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained after four immunizations significantly enhanced skin and lung fibrosis (p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained after four immunizations induced skin and lung fibrosis even in wild-type mice not immunized with topo I.
source: Remarkably, adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained after four immunizations induced skin and lung fibrosis even in wild-type mice not immunized with topo I (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis in Figures 6C and D.

claim: Skin and lung fibrosis was abrogated by administration of neutralizing antibodies against IL-6 or IL-23.
source: Skin and lung fibrosis was abrogated by administration of neutralizing antibodies against IL-6 or IL-23 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by antibody blocking experiments in Figure 6E.

claim: Adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained from IL-6 or IL-23-deficient mice immunized with topo I four times into non-immunized wild-type mice did not induce skin and lung fibrosis.
source: Similarly, adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells obtained from IL-6 or IL-23-deficient mice immunized with topo I four times into non-immunized wild-type mice did not induce skin and lung fibrosis (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments using cytokine-deficient mice in Figure 6F.

claim: Adoptive transfer experiments of B cell-specific Blimp1 CKO mice (PRDM1 CKO) induced skin sclerosis and lung fibrosis.
source: Adoptive transfer experiments of B cell-specific Blimp1 CKO mice (PRDM1 CKO) induced skin sclerosis and lung fibrosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adoptive transfer experiments of B cell-specific class II CKO mice (class II CKO) did not induce skin thickening or lung fibrosis.
source: On the other hand, adoptive transfer experiments of B cell-specific class II CKO mice (class II CKO) did not induce skin thickening or lung fibrosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The B-T interaction is important in the topo I-induced SSc model.
source: These results suggest that the B-T interaction is important in this model (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of PRDM1 CKO and class II CKO B cells in adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: BTK inhibition resulted in the decreased number and affinity for topo I of topo I-reactive B cells.
source: Thus, BTK inhibition resulted in the decreased number and affinity for topo I of topo I-reactive B cells, which was associated with increased production of anti-inflammatory cytokines and attenuated fibrosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the BTK inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells were significantly reduced in mice treated with ibrutinib compared to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.05).
source: When ibrutinib, a BTK inhibitor, was administrated in the topo I-induced SSc model mice generated by four times immunization with topo I, frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells were significantly reduced, and skin and lung fibrosis was also attenuated compared to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.05, respectively; Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and histological analysis in Figures 7A and B.

claim: Skin and lung fibrosis was attenuated in mice treated with ibrutinib compared to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.05).
source: When ibrutinib, a BTK inhibitor, was administrated in the topo I-induced SSc model mice generated by four times immunization with topo I, frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells were significantly reduced, and skin and lung fibrosis was also attenuated compared to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.05, respectively; Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: There was no difference in serum topo I antibody titer between groups treated with or without BTK inhibitors.
source: There was no difference in serum topo I antibody titer between groups treated with or without BTK inhibitors (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the serum antibody measurements in Figure 7B.

claim: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor exhibited significantly lower affinity for topo I relative to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.005).
source: Furthermore, topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor exhibited significantly lower affinity for topo I relative to the model mice without the BTK inhibitor (p<0.005; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell affinity measurements in Figure 7B.

claim: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor had higher frequencies of IL-10 and IL-35-producing cells.
source: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor had higher frequencies of IL-10 and IL-35-producing cells and also produced the significantly higher amount of IL-10 and IL-35 (p<0.005; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the cytokine analysis in Figures 7C and D.

claim: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor produced significantly higher amounts of IL-10 and IL-35 (p<0.005).
source: Topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells in the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor had higher frequencies of IL-10 and IL-35-producing cells and also produced the significantly higher amount of IL-10 and IL-35 (p<0.005; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the cytokine analysis in Figures 7C and D.

claim: Frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells producing IL-6 and IL-23 were lower in the BTK inhibitor-treated model mice with significantly lower protein expression of IL-6 and IL-23 (p<0.005).
source: By contrast, frequencies of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells producing IL-6 and IL-23 were lower in the BTK inhibitor-treated model mice with significantly lower protein expression of IL-6 and IL-23 (p<0.005; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the cytokine analysis in Figures 7C and D.

claim: Adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor failed to induce skin and lung fibrosis in non-immunized WT mice.
source: In addition, adoptive transfer of topo I-APC+ topo I-PE+ CD19+ cells from the topo I-induced SSc model mice treated with the BTK inhibitor failed to induce skin and lung fibrosis in non-immunized WT mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments in Figure 7E.

claim: For the 10 SSc patients who received RTX treatment, data at 1 year after RTX showed that mRSS improved by an average of about six points, while anti-topo I antibody titer remained the same.
source: For the 10 SSc patients who received RTX treatment, data at 1 year after RTX showed that mRSS improved by an average of about six points, while anti-topo I antibody titer remained the same (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the clinical data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rituximab (RTX), an anti-CD20 antibody that eliminates B cells, has shown efficacy in many autoimmune diseases.
source: In fact, rituximab (RTX), an anti-CD20 antibody that eliminates B cells, has shown efficacy in many autoimmune diseases, strongly suggesting that B cells are clinically important in the development of autoimmune diseases (Randall, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Randall, 2016.

claim: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a poor prognosis disease characterized by three main features: fibrosis in the skin and visceral organs, especially the lung, vasculopathy, and immune abnormalities.
source: Systemic sclerosis (SSc), one of the autoimmune diseases, is a poor prognosis disease characterized by three main features: fibrosis in the skin and visceral organs, especially the lung, vasculopathy, and immune abnormalities (Yoshizaki and Sato, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yoshizaki and Sato, 2015.

claim: Autoantibodies to nuclear antigens, such as topoisomerase (topo) I and centromere (CENP), are detected in SSc patients even before fibrosis and vasculopathy become apparent.
source: Autoantibodies to nuclear antigens, such as topoisomerase (topo) I and centromere (CENP), are detected in SSc patients even before fibrosis and vasculopathy become apparent (Burbelo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Burbelo et al., 2019.

claim: Anti-topo I antibody is linked to a severe form of SSc, while anti-CENP Ab is often accompanied by a milder form of SSc.
source: Autoantibody specificities are closely associated with SSc subsets: anti-topo I antibody is linked to a severe form of SSc, while anti-CENP Ab is often accompanied by a milder form of SSc (Kayser and Fritzler, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kayser and Fritzler, 2015.

claim: Autoantibodies are not thought to contribute to tissue damage in SSc.
source: Therefore, autoantibodies are not thought to contribute to tissue damage in SSc (Sato et al., 2004b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 2004b.

claim: Improvement of fibrosis following B cell depletion by an anti-CD20 antibody is observed in SSc even before serum autoantibody levels are reduced.
source: However, autoreactive B cells themselves are expected to play a role in the SSc pathogenesis, independent of autoantibody production; indeed, improvement of fibrosis following B cell depletion by an anti-CD20 antibody is observed in SSc even before serum autoantibody levels are reduced (Ebata et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ebata et al., 2021.

claim: Memory B cells, including autoreactive memory B cells, are abnormally activated in SSc patients.
source: In addition, memory B cells, including autoreactive memory B cells, are abnormally activated in SSc patients (Tsuchiya et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsuchiya et al., 2004.

claim: Induction of an autoimmune response to topo I causes skin and lung fibrosis characteristic of SSc in mice.
source: Studies in mice have also shown that induction of an autoimmune response to topo I causes skin and lung fibrosis characteristic of SSc (Yoshizaki et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yoshizaki et al., 2011 and Maier et al., 2017.

claim: In many autoimmune diseases, the CD27+ B cell fraction, memory B cells, is enriched with autoantigen-reactive B cells.
source: In many autoimmune diseases, the CD27+ B cell fraction, memory B cells, is enriched with autoantigen-reactive B cells (Matsumoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matsumoto et al., 2014.

claim: CD27+ B cells are highly activated in SSc.
source: CD27+ B cells are also highly activated in SSc (Sato et al., 2004a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sato et al., 2004a.

claim: The responsiveness of B cells to antigens is defined by the affinity of the B cell receptor (BCR) to antigens.
source: Moreover, the responsiveness of B cells to antigens is defined by the affinity of the B cell receptor (BCR) to antigens (Liu et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2010.

claim: Autoantigen-reactive B cells may have different affinities for an autoantigen via a different degree of somatic hypermutation.
source: and autoantigen-reactive B cells may also have the different affinities for an autoantigen via a different degree of somatic hypermutation (Elliott et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elliott et al., 2018.

claim: The volume of conventional cell culture plates is more than 106 times larger than that of cells.
source: However, the volume of conventional cell culture plates is more than 106 times larger than that of cells, which means that the conventional device size is too large for the reaction field of the small number of cells.
evidence: This is a calculation based on known volumes of cells and culture plates.

claim: BTK plays an important role in intracellular signal transduction pathways from BCR stimulation to AID activation.
source: BTK plays an important role in intracellular signal transduction pathways from BCR stimulation to AID activation, and BTK inhibitors suppress somatic hypermutation of BCR by indirectly inhibiting AID activation (Halcomb et al., 2008; Morande et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Halcomb et al., 2008 and Morande et al., 2019.

claim: BTK inhibitors suppress somatic hypermutation of BCR by indirectly inhibiting AID activation.
source: BTK plays an important role in intracellular signal transduction pathways from BCR stimulation to AID activation, and BTK inhibitors suppress somatic hypermutation of BCR by indirectly inhibiting AID activation (Halcomb et al., 2008; Morande et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Halcomb et al., 2008 and Morande et al., 2019.

claim: A large clinical trial using tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, showed a significant inhibitory effect on the progression of lung fibrosis in SSc.
source: In SSc, a large clinical trial using tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, was recently conducted and showed a significant inhibitory effect on the progression of lung fibrosis (Khanna et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Khanna et al., 2016.

claim: IL-6 enhances collagen production by fibroblasts and directly induces fibrosis.
source: IL-6 enhances collagen production by fibroblasts and directly induces fibrosis (Dufour et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dufour et al., 2018.

claim: It has been suggested that IL-6 produced by B cells is particularly important in SSc.
source: Various cells, including macrophages, produce IL-6, but it has been suggested that IL-6 produced by B cells is particularly important in SSc (Yoshizaki, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yoshizaki, 2016.

claim: Multiple subsets of B cells that produce IL-10, including CD24hi CD27+ B cells, a memory B cell phenotype, have been reported and are collectively referred to as regulatory B cells.
source: Multiple subsets of B cells that produce IL-10, including CD24hi CD27+ B cells, a memory B cell phenotype, have been reported and are collectively referred to as regulatory B cells (Mauri and Menon, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mauri and Menon, 2017.

claim: Regulatory B cells should be regarded by their suppressive function in the immune system rather than by lineage or process of differentiation.
source: As there is no specific phenotype signature for regulatory B cells, they should be regarded by their suppressive function in the immune system rather than by lineage or process of differentiation (Wąsik et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wąsik et al., 2018.

claim: B cell depletion therapy has been shown to be effective for SSc.
source: Recently, B cell depletion therapy has been shown to be effective for SSc (Yoshizaki, 2016; Yoshizaki and Sato, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yoshizaki, 2016 and Yoshizaki and Sato, 2015.

claim: The effectiveness of B cell depletion therapy varies from patient to patient.
source: Its effectiveness varies from patient to patient (Mohammed et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mohammed et al., 2017.

claim: Decreased and increased affinities for topoisomerase I of topoisomerase I-reactive B cells led to anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory cytokine production associated with the inhibition and development of fibrosis.
source: Decreased and increased affinities for topoisomerase I of topoisomerase I-reactive B cells led to anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory cytokine production associated with the inhibition and development of fibrosis, which is the major symptom of systemic sclerosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production and increased affinity of topoisomerase I-reactive B cells suppressed fibrosis.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production and increased affinity of topoisomerase I-reactive B cells suppressed fibrosis.
evidence: This is supported by the antibody blocking and BTK inhibitor experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Autoantigen-reactive B cells contribute to the disease manifestations in autoimmune disease through their antigen affinity.
source: These results indicate that autoantigen-reactive B cells contribute to the disease manifestations in autoimmune disease through their antigen affinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: Cognate interaction of B and T cells takes place primarily in spatially restricted lymphoid follicles in vivo.
source: In vivo, cognate interaction of B and T cells takes place primarily in spatially restricted lymphoid follicles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B-T cell interactions in the immune system.

claim: The microspace device used in this study mimics the B cell-T cell interaction space in vivo.
source: The microspace device used in this study is thought to mimic the B cell-T cell interaction space in vivo, suggesting that cytokines produced by topo I-reactive B cells directly affect T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design and results of the microculture experiments.

claim: Cytokines produced by topo I-reactive B cells directly affect T cell differentiation.
source: The microspace device used in this study is thought to mimic the B cell-T cell interaction space in vivo, suggesting that cytokines produced by topo I-reactive B cells directly affect T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by the microculture experiments showing T cell differentiation effects in Figure 3.

claim: The current study is the first to identify autoreactive memory B cells with low affinity for topo I that produce IL-10 in human SSc.
source: The current study is the first to identify autoreactive memory B cells with low affinity for topo I that produce IL-10 in human SSc (Figures 2 and 3), which may be regarded as regulatory autoreactive B cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, supported by the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Regulatory autoreactive B cells have inhibitory functions and may form one of the defense mechanisms that suppress the progression of fibrosis at an early stage.
source: In the SSc model mice, adoptive transfer of these regulatory autoreactive B cells attenuated fibrosis (Figure 6), indicating that regulatory autoreactive B cells have inhibitory functions and may form one of the defense mechanisms that suppress the progression of fibrosis at an early stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the adoptive transfer experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Upon further exposure to topo I, regulatory autoreactive B cells may transform into pathogenic autoreactive B cells with high affinity for topo I, resulting in the development of fibrosis.
source: However, upon further exposure to topo I, these cells may transform into pathogenic autoreactive B cells with high affinity for topo I, resulting in the development of fibrosis (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the sequential immunization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The therapeutic effect of B cell depletion therapy may be determined by relative abundance of pathogenic B cells with high affinity for topo I.
source: Its effectiveness varies from patient to patient (Mohammed et al., 2017), suggesting that the therapeutic effect may be determined by relative abundance of pathogenic B cells with high affinity for topo I.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and cited clinical observations.

claim: BTK would be a potential therapeutic target for SSc.
source: Our results also demonstrate that inhibition of affinity maturation to topo I by BTK inhibitors induced regulatory autoreactive B cells and thereby suppressed skin and lung fibrosis (Figure 7), suggesting that BTK would be a potential therapeutic target for SSc.
evidence: This is speculation based on the BTK inhibitor experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Cytokine elimination therapy targeting IL-6 and IL-23 produced by pathogenic B cells with high affinity for topo I could be new treatments for SSc.
source: On the other hand, cytokine elimination therapy targeting IL-6 and IL-23 produced by pathogenic B cells with high affinity for topo I could also be new treatments for SSc (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the cytokine blocking experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Cytokines produced by B cells, rather than antibody production from B cells, are important in the mechanism of action of BTK inhibitors in the pathogenesis of SSc.
source: These results suggest that cytokines produced by B cells, rather than antibody production from B cells, are important in the mechanism of action of BTK inhibitors in the pathogenesis of SSc, such as skin sclerosis and ILD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that BTK inhibitors reduced fibrosis without changing antibody titers.

claim: The strategy used in this study can be applied to other autoimmune diseases.
source: The strategy used in this study can be applied to other autoimmune diseases, which may pave the way for the elucidation of the mechanisms of other autoimmune diseases and the development of new treatments.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the methods.
